items.title: Introduction & Chronology
items.body:
## Indus Valley Civilization (IVC)

- The **earliest known urban culture** in the north-western part of the Indian subcontinent.
- Recognised as one of the **world's first three civilizations**, alongside **Mesopotamia** and **ancient Egypt**.
- Flourished from approximately **3300 BCE to 1300 BCE** (dated using **radiocarbon dating**).
- Its development was aided by geographic factors — **fertile soil, favourable climate** and distinct landscapes; the broad plains bordering the Indus were made fertile by annual floods leaving rich **alluvial soil**.
- Also called the **Harappan Culture** (Harappa was the first site excavated) and the **Indus–Sarasvati Civilization**; the modern name derives from the valley of the **Indus River**.
- Divided into **four phases**: **Pre-Harappan → Early Harappan → Mature Harappan → Late Harappan**.
- **Mature (urban) phase:** c. **2600–1900 BCE** (current NCERT); it was a **Bronze Age / Chalcolithic** culture — copper was used, but **iron was unknown** (early iron appears only c. 1000 BCE, after the civilization).

figure.alt: Timeline of IVC phases: Early ~3300–2600, Mature 2600–1900, Late 1900–1300 BCE
figure.caption: The three broad phases of the Harappan civilization (dates BCE).

keyPoints: Earliest urban culture of the north-western subcontinent; one of the world's first three civilizations.
Flourished c. 3300–1300 BCE (radiocarbon); mature/urban phase c. 2600–1900 BCE per NCERT.
Also called the Harappan Culture (Harappa was excavated first) and the Indus–Sarasvati Civilization.
A Bronze Age / Chalcolithic culture — iron was unknown.
Four phases: Pre-Harappan → Early → Mature → Late Harappan.
items.mnemonic: "HIM-3" — Harappan, Indus–Sarasvati, Mesopotamia+Egypt peers, 3 first civilizations.
items.source: NCERT Class XII, 'Bricks, Beads and Bones' (mature phase 2600–1900 BCE; Chalcolithic/copper, iron later) — https://ncert.nic.in/textbook/pdf/lehs101.pdf; also local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: IVC (Introduction; Origin & Discovery: 3300–1300 BCE, four phases)

items.title: Discovery & Excavators
items.body:
## Discovery of the IVC

- The Indus civilization developed in the basin of the **Indus River** from settlements practising irrigated agriculture on the Mesopotamian model.
- The first person to come across **Harappa** was **Charles Masson**, who identified it as an ancient city called **Sangala**, belonging to the time of Alexander.
- **Alexander Cunningham** — first **Director-General of the ASI** and the 'father of Indian archaeology' — noted as early as 1875 that Harappa's bricks were being robbed for railway ballast.
- In **1924, John Marshall** (Director-General of the ASI) announced to the world the existence of an ancient civilization in the Indus Valley.
- **Daya Ram Sahni** excavated **Harappa** (1920–21); **Rakhaldas Banerjee** excavated **Mohenjo-daro** (1921–22).
- **R. E. M. Wheeler** (DG ASI, 1944) introduced **stratigraphic** excavation at Harappa in **1947**.
- Figures of moisture-loving plants and animals on the seals suggest the ancient climate was **fairly moderate**, unlike the arid conditions of the region today.
keyPoints: Charles Masson first came across Harappa, calling it 'Sangala'.
Alexander Cunningham — first Director-General of the ASI, 'father of Indian archaeology'.
John Marshall announced the discovery to the world in 1924.
Daya Ram Sahni (Harappa) and Rakhaldas Banerjee (Mohenjo-daro) led the early 1920s digs.
R. E. M. Wheeler introduced stratigraphy at Harappa in 1947.
items.mnemonic: Discovery order "M-C-M-S/B-W": Masson (spots) → Cunningham (surveys) → Marshall (announces) → Sahni/Banerjee (excavate) → Wheeler (stratigraphy).
items.source: NCERT Class XII, 'Bricks, Beads and Bones' (Cunningham first DG ASI, 1875; Marshall 1924; Wheeler stratigraphy 1947) — https://ncert.nic.in/textbook/pdf/lehs101.pdf; also local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: IVC (Origin & Discovery: Masson/Sahni/Banerjee)

items.title: Geographical Extent & Boundary Sites
items.body:
## Extent of the Civilization

- Situated in the river basins of the **Indus** and the **Ghaggar–Hakra**.
- Encompassed an area of approximately **1,299,600 sq km (~1.3 million sq km)** — considerably larger than the contemporary Egyptian or Mesopotamian cultures.
- Extended beyond the Indus zone into riverine lowlands of **Uttar Pradesh and Rajasthan**, highlands and coastal parts of **Balochistan**, and a coastal strip in **Gujarat**.

### Boundary sites
- **West:** Sutkagendor (Balochistan, Pakistan)
- **East:** Alamgirpur (Uttar Pradesh)
- **North:** Manda (Jammu; on the Chenab)
- **South:** Daimabad (Maharashtra)

figure.alt: Schematic map of major IVC sites and the four cardinal boundary sites
figure.caption: Major sites and the boundary sites: Manda (N), Alamgirpur (E), Sutkagendor (W), Daimabad (S).

keyPoints: Spread over ~1.3 million sq km — larger than contemporary Egypt or Mesopotamia.
Boundary sites: Manda (North), Alamgirpur (East), Sutkagendor (West), Daimabad (South).
Centred on the Indus and Ghaggar–Hakra river basins.
Northernmost Manda lies on the Chenab; southern boundary Daimabad is the standard modern key.
items.mnemonic: Boundaries N-E-W-S = "MASD": Manda, Alamgirpur, Sutkagendor, Daimabad.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: IVC (Map & Sites; Area ~1,299,600 sq km; boundary sites). Site names (Manda, Sutkagendor, Balakot, etc.) also on the NCERT Class XII 'Bricks, Beads and Bones' Mature-Harappan map — https://ncert.nic.in/textbook/pdf/lehs101.pdf

items.title: Major Sites & Their Findings
items.body:
## Major Indus Valley Sites

- **Harappa** (Punjab, Pakistan; **Ravi** river): sandstone statues of human anatomy, a **gateway city** and meeting point of routes, **granaries**, bullock carts.
- **Mohenjo-daro** (Sindh, Pakistan; **Indus** river): the **Great Bath**, a collegiate building and assembly hall, a granary, the **Bronze Dancing Girl**, the **unicorn seal**, **cotton**, and the **Pashupati Mahadeva (proto-Siva) seal**.
- **Rakhigarhi** (Hisar district, Haryana; **Sarasvati** river; excavated by **Amarendra Nath**): burnt-brick houses, an effective drainage system, a mud-brick granary, and a seal bearing an alligator emblem.
- **Dholavira** (Great Rann of Kutch / Khadir island, Gujarat; discovered **1968** by **Jagat Pati Joshi**): a three-part city (citadel, middle town, lower town), a cascade of **stone water reservoirs**; the **southern centre** of the Harappan civilization; a **UNESCO World Heritage Site (2021)**, India's **40th**. Known as a **lake city / jala durga (water fort)**.
- **Lothal** (Gulf of Khambhat, Gujarat): a **tidal dockyard** and **bead factory**, the **sole port town** of the IVC; worship of the fire god; early evidence of **rice farming** in South Asia.
- **Kalibangan** (Rajasthan; **Ghaggar** river; discovered by **Amlanand Ghosh**, 1953): priest quarters, **fire pits (fire altars)**, **plough marks**, a double-cropping pattern, and a bronze bull.

figure.caption: Mohenjo-daro — the excavated grid of one of the two largest Harappan cities.

keyPoints: Harappa (Ravi) — granaries, gateway city; Mohenjo-daro (Indus) — Great Bath, Dancing Girl, Pashupati seal, cotton.
Rakhigarhi (Sarasvati, Haryana; Amarendra Nath) — drainage, mud-brick granary.
Dholavira (Kutch) — cascading stone reservoirs, three-part city, southern centre; UNESCO 2021, India's 40th.
Lothal (Gujarat) — tidal dockyard, bead factory, sole port; early rice.
Kalibangan (Ghaggar, Rajasthan) — fire altars, plough marks, double cropping.
items.mnemonic: Site→river "HR-MI-KG-RS": Harappa–Ravi, Mohenjo-daro–Indus, Kalibangan–Ghaggar, Rakhigarhi–Sarasvati.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: IVC (Major Sites table); Great Bath / steatite / Pashupati per NCERT Class XII 'Bricks, Beads and Bones' — https://ncert.nic.in/textbook/pdf/lehs101.pdf; Dholavira (southern centre, Khadir/Gujarat, UNESCO 2021) per UNESCO — https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1645/

items.title: Other Notable Sites
items.body:
## Other Important Sites

- **Chanhudaro** (Sindh, Pakistan; Indus; N. G. Majumdar, 1931): a **bead-making factory**; notable for having **no citadel**.
- **Banawali** (Haryana; Ghaggar; R. S. Bisht, 1974): fortified town, terracotta figurines, evidence of **cotton cultivation**, a toy/terracotta plough.
- **Surkotada** (Gujarat; J. P. Joshi, 1964): a fortified settlement and copper objects; noted for **reported horse remains**.
- **Alamgirpur** (Uttar Pradesh; Hindon; Y. D. Sharma, 1958): late-Harappan pottery; the **easternmost** extent of the IVC.
- **Sutkagendor** (Balochistan; Dasht; Aurel Stein, 1929): a fortified town near the Arabian Sea; a **trade link** between Harappa and Mesopotamia; the **westernmost** site.
- **Daimabad** (Maharashtra; Pravara; B. K. Thapar, 1958): **bronze sculptures** showing Harappan influence in the Deccan; the **southernmost** site.
- **Manda** (Jammu; Chenab; ASI, 1947): the **northernmost** Harappan site.
- Others include **Rangpur** (rice cultivation), **Mitathal**, **Bhagatrav** (a Harappan port and bead-making centre), and **Balakot** (shell working).
keyPoints: Chanhudaro (Sindh) — bead factory and, unusually, no citadel.
Banawali — cotton, terracotta figurines, a toy plough; Surkotada — reported horse remains.
Boundary sites: Sutkagendor (W), Alamgirpur (E), Manda (N), Daimabad (S).
Coastal shell/port sites include Balakot and Bhagatrav.
items.mnemonic: "No-citadel bead town = Chanhudaro"; reported horse remains = Surkotada.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: IVC (Other Important sites table); Chanhudaro, Banawali, Balakot and Rangpur also appear on the NCERT Class XII 'Bricks, Beads and Bones' map — https://ncert.nic.in/textbook/pdf/lehs101.pdf

items.title: Town Planning & the Grid Layout
items.body:
## Town Planning

- Cities followed a **rectangular grid pattern**; main **roads met at right angles**.
- The grid roads divided into smaller roads that connected to the **lanes of individual houses**.
- Construction used **burnt (baked) mud bricks**, cut to a standardised **4:2:1** ratio (length : breadth : thickness — the length and breadth being four times and twice the height) — **uniform across sites**.
- Structures included dwelling houses, **public buildings**, and **public baths**.
- The uniform, standardised layout across a vast area points to **centralised civic planning**.

figures.alt: Diagram of a Harappan town: citadel to the west, gridded lower town to the east
figures.caption: Schematic Harappan town plan — raised citadel (west) and gridded lower town (east).

figures.alt: Right-angled street grid excavated at Mohenjo-daro
figures.caption: The excavated grid of streets at Mohenjo-daro.

keyPoints: Rectangular grid; main roads meet at right angles, lanes branch to houses.
Burnt bricks in a standardised 4:2:1 (L:B:T) ratio, uniform across sites.
Cities split into a raised citadel (west) and a lower town (east).
Uniform layout over a vast area implies centralised civic planning.
items.mnemonic: "GC-421": Grid roads, Citadel-west, brick ratio 4:2:1.
items.source: NCERT Class XII, 'Bricks, Beads and Bones' (standardised 4:2:1 bricks — length & breadth four and two times the height) — https://ncert.nic.in/textbook/pdf/lehs101.pdf; also local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: IVC (Art & Architecture — Town Planning)

items.title: Citadel, Lower Town & Granaries
items.body:
## City Division

- Each city was divided into an **upraised citadel** (to the west) and a **lower part** (to the east).
- **Citadel:** housed **granaries**, administrative buildings, courtyards and **pillared halls**.
- **Lower town:** small **one-room quarters** for working-class people, and public baths (e.g. the **Great Bath** at Mohenjo-daro).
- **Granaries** were among the notable public structures — found at **Harappa** and **Mohenjo-daro**; at Rakhigarhi the granary was made of **mud bricks** with a rammed-earth floor plastered with mud.

figure.alt: Cutaway diagram of a Harappan granary with air ducts and loading platform
figure.caption: A Harappan granary — a key public structure on the citadel.

keyPoints: Citadel (west, raised): granaries, administrative buildings, pillared halls, courtyards.
Lower town (east): one-room workers' quarters and public baths.
Granaries found at Harappa and Mohenjo-daro; Rakhigarhi's was mud-brick.
The citadel/lower-town split reflects planned zoning of the city.
items.mnemonic: "West = Watchful citadel; East = Everyday homes."
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: IVC (Art & Architecture — City Division); the citadel/lower-town division and the Great Bath are also described in NCERT Class XII 'Bricks, Beads and Bones' — https://ncert.nic.in/textbook/pdf/lehs101.pdf

items.title: The Great Bath, Drainage & Sanitation
items.body:
## Water Management & Sanitation

### The Great Bath
- A large watertight public tank (a large rectangular tank in a courtyard) on the **citadel at Mohenjo-daro** — the best-known public structure of the IVC. It is found **only at Mohenjo-daro** (a common trap is to place it at Harappa).

### Drainage system
- **Small drains** from each house connected to **larger drains** running alongside the main roads.
- Drains were **covered loosely** to allow regular cleaning and maintenance; at some sites the street drains were **laid before the houses**.
- **Cesspits** were placed at **regular intervals**.
- This networked, covered drainage reflects an advanced sense of **hygiene and civic sanitation** — a hallmark of the civilization.

figures.alt: The Great Bath at Mohenjo-daro — a large sunken brick tank
figures.caption: The Great Bath, Mohenjo-daro — a watertight tank on the citadel.

figures.alt: Covered brick street drains of a Harappan city
figures.caption: Covered street drains — the hallmark of Harappan sanitation.

keyPoints: The Great Bath is a watertight citadel tank at Mohenjo-daro — only there.
House drains fed covered street drains, loosely covered for cleaning.
Cesspits at regular intervals; drains sometimes laid before the houses.
Advanced covered drainage is a hallmark of Harappan civic sanitation.
items.mnemonic: "Great Bath = Mohenjo-daro ONLY" — never Harappa.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: IVC (City Division; Drainage System — Great Bath at the Mohenjodaro site); the Great Bath is also described in NCERT Class XII 'Bricks, Beads and Bones' — https://ncert.nic.in/textbook/pdf/lehs101.pdf

items.title: Economy, Trade, Weights & Measures
items.body:
## Economy & Trade

- **Occupations:** weaving of cloth, **bead-making** (clay, stone, paste, shell, ivory), **metalwork**, and trade.
- **Trade partners:** the **Persian Gulf** and the **Sumerians**; seals and small objects of Mohenjo-daro have been found at sites in **Iraq (Mesopotamia)**.
- Trade with **Afghanistan** is traced for the blue gemstone **lapis lazuli**.
- It was a **barter economy** — no coins were used.
- **Weights and measures:** found at the **Lothal dock** in various shapes and were **accurate**, indicating a regulated trade system.
- **Agriculture:** primary crops were **wheat and barley**; fruits included **pomegranates and bananas**; diet also included meat and fish. Kalibangan shows **plough marks** and a **double-cropping** pattern; Lothal shows early **rice** farming.
keyPoints: Occupations: weaving, bead-making, metalwork, trade — a barter economy (no coins).
Trade with the Persian Gulf and Sumerians; seals found in Iraq (Mesopotamia).
Lapis lazuli obtained from Afghanistan; also carnelian, copper and shell.
Accurate standardised weights and measures found at the Lothal dock.
items.mnemonic: Occupations "Weave–Bead–Metal–Trade" (the four Harappan livelihoods).
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: IVC (Features — Occupations, Trade, Food habits); the precise chert weight system is detailed in NCERT Class XII 'Bricks, Beads and Bones' — https://ncert.nic.in/textbook/pdf/lehs101.pdf

items.title: Mesopotamian Contacts & Trade Toponyms
items.body:
## Mesopotamian Contacts & Trade Toponyms

- Mesopotamian texts name three lands in the maritime trade network:
  - **Meluha (NCERT: Meluhha)** = the **Indus region** (possibly the Harappan land itself).
  - **Dilmun** = **Bahrain** — an entrepôt in the Persian Gulf.
  - **Magan** = **Oman** — a source of **copper**.
- Harappan **seals and objects** have been found in **Mesopotamia (Iraq)**; **carnelian** beads and etched ornaments were prized exports.
- **Shortughai** (northern **Afghanistan**) was a Harappan **outpost** securing **lapis lazuli** and other raw materials — the **only Harappan site with traces of irrigation canals** (not found in Punjab or Sind).
- Exchange was **maritime**, via the Persian Gulf, in a **barter** system.

figure.alt: Map showing the western reach of the IVC toward the Persian Gulf and Afghanistan
figure.caption: Westward trade reach — toward the Persian Gulf (Dilmun/Magan) and Afghanistan (Shortughai).

keyPoints: Meluhha = the Indus land; Dilmun = Bahrain; Magan = Oman (copper source).
Harappan seals/objects found in Mesopotamia (Iraq) confirm long-distance trade.
Shortughai (Afghanistan) = raw-material (lapis) outpost; the only site with canal traces.
Trade was maritime, via the Persian Gulf, in a barter economy.
items.mnemonic: "Meluha–Dilmun–Magan" = India–Bahrain–Oman (My-Dear-Man).
items.source: NCERT Class XII, 'Bricks, Beads and Bones' (Dilmun/Magan/Meluhha; carnelian exports; Shortughai canal traces, not in Punjab or Sind) — https://ncert.nic.in/textbook/pdf/lehs101.pdf

items.title: Weights, Measures & Brick Standardisation
items.body:
## Standardisation — Weights, Measures & Bricks

### Weights
- Made of **chert**, usually **cubical** and **without markings**.
- **Lower denominations were binary** — 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 — while **higher ones were decimal** — 160, 200, 320, 640 (i.e. **multiples of 16**).
- Metal **scale-pans** have been found; **accurate weights** turned up at the **Lothal dock**.

### Bricks
- **Baked bricks** followed a fixed **4:2:1** ratio (length : breadth : thickness), **uniform across sites**.

### Why it matters
- The region-wide uniformity of weights and bricks is a leading argument for a **standardising central authority**.
keyPoints: Weights were chert, cubical and unmarked.
Binary in the lower range (1–32), decimal in the higher (160–640) — multiples of 16.
Accurate weights at the Lothal dock; metal scale-pans recovered.
Bricks in a standardised 4:2:1 ratio, uniform across sites.
Standard weights + bricks argue for a centralised regulating authority.
items.mnemonic: "16 & 421": weights in multiples of 16; bricks 4:2:1.
items.source: NCERT Class XII, 'Bricks, Beads and Bones' (chert cubical weights, binary→decimal, 4:2:1 bricks) — https://ncert.nic.in/textbook/pdf/lehs101.pdf; Lothal weights per local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: IVC

items.title: Crafts, Seals & the Harappan Script
items.body:
## Seals & Crafts

### Seals
- Made mainly of **steatite** (a soft stone found in river beds); also of **copper, gold, faience, ivory and terracotta**.
- Shapes: **square, triangular, rectangular and circular**.
- Inscriptions were in a **pictographic** script written **right to left** — still **undeciphered**; inscriptions are short (the **longest ~26 signs**), and the script has **~375–400 signs** (so it was not alphabetic).
- The **unicorn (one-horned bull)** is a common motif — often a mythical, composite creature; some seals bear a bull, and some a half-man, half-animal figure (the **Pashupati seal**); the **swastika** appears on some.
- **Use:** trade, identification marks and educational purposes.

### Bronze & other crafts
- **Bronze** was cast by the **cire perdue (lost-wax) method** — e.g. the **Dancing Girl**.
- **Beads** were made of clay, stone, paste, shell and ivory; **cotton** and wool were woven for cloth.

figures.alt: Close-up of a Harappan seal showing pictographic script and an animal motif
figures.caption: A Harappan seal — pictographic script (right-to-left) above an animal motif.

figures.alt: The Pashupati seal showing a seated horned figure surrounded by animals
figures.caption: The Pashupati seal — a half-man/half-animal (proto-Siva) figure.

keyPoints: Seals mostly steatite; also copper, gold, faience, ivory, terracotta.
Script pictographic, right-to-left, undeciphered; ~375–400 signs, longest inscription ~26 signs.
The 'unicorn' (one-horned bull) is a common seal motif; Pashupati seal is half-man/half-animal.
Bronzes cast by cire perdue (lost-wax), e.g. the Dancing Girl.
items.mnemonic: Seals = "SRUU": Steatite, Right-to-left, Undeciphered, Unicorn-motif.
items.source: NCERT Class XII, 'Bricks, Beads and Bones' (steatite seals, right-to-left, ~375–400 signs / longest ~26, undeciphered, 'unicorn' composite motif) — https://ncert.nic.in/textbook/pdf/lehs101.pdf; also local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: IVC (Sculptures — Seals; Bronze figures)

items.title: Craft Specialisation & Centres
items.body:
## Craft Specialisation & Centres

- **Chanhudaro** (Sindh) — a **tiny site (< 7 ha**, vs Mohenjo-daro's **~125 ha**) that was **almost wholly a craft settlement**: **bead-making, shell-cutting, metalwork, seal-making and weight-making**; it had **no citadel**.
- **Bead materials:** **carnelian** (its red colour obtained by **firing** the yellowish raw material), jasper, crystal, quartz, steatite, faience, shell, terracotta and gold. Specialised cylindrical **drills** are known from **Chanhudaro, Lothal and Dholavira**.
- **Shell-working centres:** **Nageshwar** and **Balakot**, near the coast.
- **Cotton:** traces of cotton are attested at Harappan sites.
- **Gold jewellery** at Harappan sites was generally recovered from **hoards**.

figure.alt: Harappan beads and jewellery of carnelian, steatite and gold
figure.caption: Harappan beads and ornaments — carnelian, steatite, faience, shell and gold.

keyPoints: Chanhudaro (< 7 ha, no citadel) — a specialised craft town: beads, shell, metal, seals, weights.
Carnelian beads reddened by firing; specialised drills at Chanhudaro, Lothal, Dholavira.
Shell-working centres: Nageshwar and Balakot.
Cotton is attested at Harappan sites; gold jewellery was recovered from hoards.
items.mnemonic: Shell = "N-B" (Nageshwar, Balakot); crafts hub = Chanhudaro.
items.source: NCERT Class XII, 'Bricks, Beads and Bones' (Chanhudaro <7 ha vs Mohenjodaro 125 ha, drills, carnelian reddened by firing, Nageshwar/Balakot shell, cotton traces, gold from hoards) — https://ncert.nic.in/textbook/pdf/lehs101.pdf

items.title: Subsistence — Crops, Diet & Animals
items.body:
## Subsistence — Crops, Diet & Animals

- **Crops:** **wheat, barley, lentil, chickpea and sesame**; **millets** at Gujarat sites; **rice** was relatively rare (early evidence at **Lothal / Rangpur**).
- **Animals (archaeozoology):** bones of domesticated **cattle, sheep, goat, buffalo and pig**; wild species and **fish** were eaten.
- **Agricultural technology:** the **bull on seals** implies **oxen-drawn ploughing**; **terracotta plough models** come from **Cholistan and Banawali**; a **ploughed field** with two right-angled furrow sets (two crops) was found at **Kalibangan**.
- **Irrigation canals** are attested only at **Shortughai (Afghanistan)**, not in the Punjab–Sindh core.
keyPoints: Staples: wheat, barley, lentil, chickpea, sesame; millets in Gujarat; rice rare.
Domesticated cattle, sheep, goat, buffalo, pig; also fish (archaeozoology).
Oxen ploughing (bull seals); terracotta plough models at Cholistan and Banawali.
Earliest ploughed field at Kalibangan; irrigation canals only at Shortughai.
items.mnemonic: Crops "We Bring Lentils, Chickpeas, Sesame" — Wheat, Barley, Lentil, Chickpea, Sesame.
items.source: NCERT Class XII, 'Bricks, Beads and Bones' (crops incl. millets in Gujarat & rice rare, animal bones, plough models at Cholistan/Banawali, Kalibangan ploughed field, Shortughai canals) — https://ncert.nic.in/textbook/pdf/lehs101.pdf; Lothal rice per local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: IVC

items.title: Religion, Beliefs & Burial Practices
items.body:
## Religion & Beliefs

- Terracotta figurines of heavily jewelled **women**, some with elaborate head-dresses, are regarded as **Mother Goddesses**; rare stone statuary of seated men also occurs.
- A seated, horned figure on a seal, sometimes surrounded by animals, has been regarded as a depiction of **'proto-Shiva' (Pashupati)** — shown seated on a low throne with animals around him. (NCERT cautions that, unlike Shiva, the Rigvedic Rudra is neither called Pashupati nor shown as a yogi, so the identification is **not straightforward**.)
- In the APPSC source the four animals around the figure are given as **elephant, tiger, rhinoceros and buffalo**.
- Sacred objects included the **Peepal tree seal** and the **Horned Bull seal**.
- **No temples** have been conclusively identified.
- Structures assigned ritual significance include the **Great Bath** and the **fire altars** found at **Kalibangan and Lothal**.

### Burial practices (three types, per the APPSC source)
1. **Extended burial** — the body placed in a North–South direction.
2. **Symbolic burial** — no body found (e.g. **Kalibangan**).
3. **Twin burial** — two bodies in one grave (e.g. a man and a dog).

figures.alt: The Pashupati (proto-Siva) seal, a seated horned deity flanked by animals
figures.caption: Pashupati (proto-Siva) — flanked by elephant, tiger, rhinoceros and buffalo.

figures.alt: A Harappan extended burial with grave goods
figures.caption: An extended (N–S) Harappan burial with grave goods.

keyPoints: Mother Goddess terracotta figures; seated 'proto-Shiva' (Pashupati) seal (identification not straightforward).
The APPSC source lists Pashupati's four animals: elephant, tiger, rhinoceros, buffalo.
Sacred Peepal tree and Horned Bull; Great Bath and fire altars (Kalibangan, Lothal); no temples identified.
Three burials (APPSC source): extended (N–S), symbolic (Kalibangan), twin (man and dog).
items.mnemonic: Pashupati's animals "ETRB" (Elephant, Tiger, Rhino, Buffalo); burials "EST" (Extended, Symbolic, Twin).
items.source: NCERT Class XII, 'Bricks, Beads and Bones' (mother goddesses, 'proto-Shiva' reading and its caveats, Great Bath & fire altars at Kalibangan/Lothal) — https://ncert.nic.in/textbook/pdf/lehs101.pdf; four animals & burial types per local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: IVC (Features — Religion; burial types)

items.title: Art & Sculpture
items.body:
## Art & Sculpture

- **Bronze — the Dancing Girl:** cast by the **cire perdue (lost-wax)** technique and shown in the **tribhanga** posture; from **Mohenjo-daro**.
- **Stone — the Bearded Priest ('Priest-King'):** draped in a shawl with **trefoil patterns**; the eyes are elongated and half-closed as if in **meditation**; also from **Mohenjo-daro**. A red sandstone **male torso** is another fine example.
- **Terracotta:** fire-baked clay used for toys, animal figures, miniature carts and wheels.
- **Pottery:** wheel-made, in **plain** and **painted** forms. Painted pottery — the **Red and Black ware** — used a red background with black designs (trees, birds, animals and geometric patterns); used for household, decorative and liquor-pouring purposes.
- Note: both the **Dancing Girl** and the **'Priest-King'** are from **Mohenjo-daro** — a common swap trap.

keyPoints: Bronze Dancing Girl — cire perdue, tribhanga posture (Mohenjo-daro).
Stone 'Priest-King' — trefoil shawl, meditative half-closed eyes (Mohenjo-daro).
Terracotta toys/figurines; wheel-made Red-and-Black painted pottery.

items.title: Society & Daily Life
items.body:
## Society & Livelihood

- **Food:** wheat and barley were the main crops; fruits included pomegranates and bananas; the diet also had meat and fish.
- **Costume:** clothes were mostly of **wool and cotton**; women wore a short skirt while men wrapped a long piece of cloth.
- **Ornaments:** women wore bracelets and necklaces of **shells, gold and silver**; men wore **amulets** for protection.
- **Amusements:** children played with small clay carts, dolls, rattles and marbles; animal puppets and bird-shaped whistles were made; older people enjoyed **gambling**.
- The **material uniformity** of goods across a vast region suggests shared cultural norms and an occupationally differentiated, prosperous society.

figure.alt: Harappan ornaments — bangles and necklaces of shell, gold and silver
figure.caption: Ornaments of shell, gold and silver — everyday Harappan adornment.

keyPoints: Staples wheat and barley; fruits pomegranate and banana; also meat and fish.
Clothing of wool and cotton; ornaments of shell, gold and silver; men wore amulets.
Toys, whistles and gambling point to a prosperous, leisured society.
Material uniformity across the region implies shared cultural norms.
items.mnemonic: "Wool + Cotton" clothed the Harappans; ornaments = Shell-Gold-Silver.

items.title: Who Ruled? The Priest-King / State Debate
items.body:
## Who Ruled? The Priest-King / State Debate

- **No temples or palaces** have been conclusively identified; a large Mohenjo-daro building once called a 'palace' yielded **no rich finds**.
- A steatite bust is conventionally labelled the **'Priest-King'** — a name borrowed by **analogy with Mesopotamia** and **not proven**; there is no clear evidence of a priestly ruler.
- The **extraordinary uniformity** of pottery, seals, weights and the **4:2:1 brick ratio** across a vast area suggests a **standardising authority**.
- Scholars debate three models: a **single state**, **several rulers / cities**, or a **relatively egalitarian** community with **no single ruler**.
- There are **no royal tombs** or monarchic iconography — authority looks unlike that of Egypt or Mesopotamia.

figure.caption: The so-called 'Priest-King' — the label is a Mesopotamian analogy, not proven.

keyPoints: No temples or palaces conclusively identified; the Mohenjo-daro 'palace' was find-poor.
The 'Priest-King' label is a Mesopotamian analogy — unproven.
Region-wide uniformity (weights, seals, 4:2:1 bricks) argues for a standardising authority.
Three models debated: single state vs several rulers vs egalitarian no-ruler society.
No royal tombs or monarchic iconography — unlike Egypt or Mesopotamia.
items.mnemonic: "No palace, No temple, No proven king — only standard bricks."
items.source: NCERT Class XII, 'Bricks, Beads and Bones' (authority debate, 'priest-king' Mesopotamian analogy, region-wide uniformity argument) — https://ncert.nic.in/textbook/pdf/lehs101.pdf

items.title: Late (Post-Urban) Harappan
items.body:
## Late (Post-Urban) Harappan

- Per NCERT, the **decline** of the civilisation begins around **1900 BCE**; the **decadent phase c. 1900–1300 BCE** is termed **Late Harappan**.
- In this phase the **distinctive Harappan features fade**: the characteristic **seals**, the **writing/script**, the **standardised weights**, **long-distance trade** and specialised **craft technologies** decline or disappear.
- Planned baked-brick urbanism and the grid layout give way to more modest, largely **rural** settlement — best read as **de-urbanisation with some cultural continuity** rather than a single sudden collapse.
- This phase follows the **Mature Harappan (c. 2600–1900 BCE)** and precedes the later iron-using Early Historic cultures.

figure.caption: Late-Harappan painted pottery — the mature urban template fades after c. 1900 BCE.

keyPoints: NCERT: decline begins ~1900 BCE; the decadent phase c. 1900–1300 BCE is 'Late Harappan'.
Distinctive seals, script, standardised weights and long-distance trade fade in this phase.
Planned brick urbanism gives way to more modest, largely rural settlement.
Best read as de-urbanisation with continuity, not an abrupt collapse.
items.mnemonic: "1900 → 1300 BCE = Late Harappan": the urban template fades, not a sudden end.
items.source: NCERT Class XII, 'Bricks, Beads and Bones' (decline ~1900 BCE; Late Harappan / decadent phase 1900–1300 BCE; loss of distinctive seals, script, weights and long-distance trade) — https://ncert.nic.in/textbook/pdf/lehs101.pdf; four-phase scheme per local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: IVC

items.title: Decline of the Harappans
items.body:
## Fall of the Harappans

- The decline is placed around **1500 BCE** in the APPSC source — the period also associated with the arrival of the **Aryans**. (Per NCERT, the distinctive urban phase already ends by c. **1900 BCE**.) There is **no conclusive evidence** for any single cause.

### Theories proposed (per the APPSC source)
1. A **massive flood** of the Indus drowning the cities; **eastward-moving monsoons** bringing destructive heavy rains.
2. Invasion by a nomadic **Indo-European tribe (the Aryans)**, coinciding with the dated decline — a proposed theory, not conclusively established.
3. **Drying of the Saraswati River** (beginning around **1900 BCE**) causing climate change and prolonged drought.
4. **Droughts leading to famines**.
5. A **pandemic disease** wiping out the population.
6. By **1800 BCE** a cooler, drier climate and a **tectonic event** may have diverted river systems, prompting **migration toward the Ganges basin**.
- Seals, script, standardised weights and long-distance trade **disappear** — best read as a **gradual, multi-causal transformation**.
keyPoints: APPSC source dates the fall ~1500 BCE; NCERT ends the urban phase by ~1900 BCE. No single agreed cause.
Environmental: Indus floods, shifting monsoons, drying Saraswati (~1900 BCE), drought and famine.
The Aryan-invasion theory is one of several proposed; the source records no conclusive evidence.
By ~1800 BCE cooler/drier climate and tectonic river shifts; migration toward the Ganga basin.
Seals, script, weights and long-distance trade fade — a gradual, multi-causal process.
items.mnemonic: Decline theories "FAST-D": Flood, Aryans, Saraswati-drying, Tectonic/climate, Disease.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: IVC (Fall of Harappans — theories; 'no conclusive evidence yet'); post-1900 BCE end of the urban phase per NCERT Class XII 'Bricks, Beads and Bones' — https://ncert.nic.in/textbook/pdf/lehs101.pdf

items.title: Odd-One-Out & Inference Facts (PYQ)
items.body:
## Frequently-tested traps and inferences

### 'Which is NOT a Harappan site?'
- **Sohgaura** (UP) is **NOT** Harappan — it is a **Mauryan copper-plate inscription** site. Genuine Harappan sites in such lists: **Chanhudaro, Kot Diji, Desalpur, Banawali, Surkotada**.

### Script & weights
- The Harappan script is **pictographic, undeciphered**, and written **right-to-left** (first line), often **boustrophedon** (alternating direction line by line). ~375–400 signs.

### Society & economy inferences
- **Spindle-whorls are common but no spinning wheels** are found → spinning was done **at home** by hand. Baked-brick houses with **wells and bathing platforms** → concern for water/hygiene, not 'scientific' knowledge of medicine.
- IVC society was **predominantly secular** (religion not dominant); **cotton** ('sindon' to Greeks) was used for textiles — the Harappans were the **first to produce cotton**.
- **Horse was absent/not central** (bones debated at Surkotada); IVC knew **copper/bronze but NOT iron**. This distinguishes them from the **Rigvedic Aryans** (who used the horse-drawn spoked-wheel chariot).

### Superlatives (current excavation status)
- **Rakhigarhi** (Haryana) is now the **largest Harappan site**, overtaking Mohenjo-daro; ancient-DNA studies here feed the Aryan-migration debate.
keyPoints: Sohgaura is NOT Harappan — it is a Mauryan copper-plate inscription site.
Script written right-to-left, often boustrophedon; undeciphered, ~375–400 signs.
Spindle-whorls but no spinning wheels → home spinning; IVC society predominantly secular; first to use cotton.
Horse absent and iron unknown — key contrast with Rigvedic Aryans.
Rakhigarhi (Haryana) is the largest Harappan site.
